FAQ question: Jupyter Notebook or SparkUI not loading properly at localhost after port forwarding from VS code?

Document (the answer, with line numbers):
1: **Possible Solution:** Try to forward the port using SSH CLI instead of VS Code. 
2: 
3: Run the following command:
4: 
5: ```bash
6: ssh -L <local port>:<VM host/ip>:<VM port> <ssh hostname>
7: ```
8: 
9: - `ssh hostname` is the name you specified in the `~/.ssh/config` file.
10: 
11: For example, in case of Jupyter Notebook, run:
12: 
13: ```bash
14: ssh -L 8888:localhost:8888 gcp-vm
15: ```
16: 
17: from your local machine’s CLI.
18: 
19: **Note:** If you logout from the session, the connection would break. While creating the Spark session, check the block's log because sometimes it fails to run at 4040 and switches to 4041.
20: 
21: If you are having trouble accessing localhost ports from a GCP VM, consider adding the forwarding instructions to the `.ssh/config` file as follows:
22: 
23: ```bash
24: Host <hostname>
25:   Hostname <external-gcp-ip>
26:   User xxxx
27:   IdentityFile yyyy
28:   LocalForward 8888 localhost:8888
29:   LocalForward 8080 localhost:8080
30:   LocalForward 5432 localhost:5432
31:   LocalForward 4040 localhost:4040
32: ```
33: 
34: This should automatically forward all ports and will enable accessing localhost ports.

FAQ question: GCP: SSH public key error - multiple users / usernames

Document (the answer, with line numbers):

2: 
3: **Permanent Solution:**
4: 
5: It turns out it wasn’t an issue with the key generation at all! The problem was with the username. I had given my SSH key a different username than what appeared in my VM (my Google account username). So, I had been trying to log in with `googleacctuser@[ipaddr]` instead of `mySSHuser@[ipaddr]`. Here's how I resolved it:
6: 
7: 1. Retraced my steps to check the SSH key setup in the GCP console, where it showed the user and SSH key.
8: 2. Changed the username to the correct one (googleacctuser) in my config file.
9: 3. Updated the config file and used `mySSHuser` to log in.
10: 
11: Now, the issue was that I had created two users. I made all the installations and permissions on `googleacctuser`, not accessible from `mySSHuser`. Since I didn't need `mySSHuser`, I edited the SSH key to change the username at the end and updated the GCP console and config file accordingly.

13: Then, I planned to delete the `mySSHuser` account in the VM terminal to keep things clean (though I got a bit attached, so I skipped this).

16:

FAQ section: Module 1: Postgres, pgAdmin & Python ingestion
FAQ question: Postgres fails to start after upgrading from postgres:16 to postgres:18 in Docker

Document (the answer, with line numbers):
1: Postgres 18 changes how the data directory is structured inside Docker containers. While Postgres ≤16 stored data under /var/lib/postgresql/data, Postgres 18 expects the volume to be mounted at /var/lib/postgresql. If an existing volume created with an older Postgres version is reused without updating the mount path, Postgres 18 will detect an incompatible layout and exit during startup. This can appear as DNS resolution errors or failed connections from pgAdmin or ingestion jobs. For Week 1 setups, the fix is to update the volume mount path, remove the old volume, and recreate the containers so Postgres 18 can initialize a new data directory.
2: 
3: **Proposed Fix (Week 1 setups)**
4: - Update the volume mount path to /var/lib/postgresql (instead of /var/lib/postgresql/data).
5: - Remove the old volume that was created with Postgres 16.
6: - Recreate the containers so Postgres 18 initializes a fresh data directory.
7: 
8: **Example commands**
9: - Running with docker run (adjust as needed):
10: ```
11: docker run -it \
12:   -e POSTGRES_USER="root" \
13:   -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD="admin" \
14:   -e POSTGRES_DB="ny_taxi" \
15:   -v "/path/to/ny_taxi_postgres_data":"/var/lib/postgresql" \
16:   -p 5432:5432 \
17:   postgres:18
18: ```
19: 
20: - For docker-compose, mount the volume to /var/lib/postgresql:
21: ```
22: volumes:
23:   ny_taxi_postgres_data:
24: 
25: services:
26:   postgres:
27:     image: postgres:18
28:     environment:
29:       POSTGRES_USER: root
30:       POSTGRES_PASSWORD: admin
31:       POSTGRES_DB: ny_taxi
32:     volumes:
33:       - ny_taxi_postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql
34: ```
35: 
36: - Remove the old volume (list and remove):
37: ```
38: docker volume ls
39: docker volume rm <old-volume-name>
40: ```
41: 
42: - Recreate containers:
43: ```
44: docker-compose down
45: docker-compose up -d
46: ```
47: 
48: - Ensure you have a backup of any important data before removing volumes.
49: - After restarting, verify that Postgres starts and the data directory is initialized under /var/lib/postgresql.

FAQ section: Module 1: Taxi Data (download & handling)
FAQ question: Taxi Data: How to handle *.csv.gz taxi data files?

Document (the answer, with line numbers):
1: In [this video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=B1WwATwf-vY&list=PL3MmuxUbc_hJed7dXYoJw8DoCuVHhGEQb), the data file is stored as `output.csv`. If the file extension is `csv.gz` instead of `csv`, it won't store correctly.
2: 
3: To handle this:
4: 
5: 1. Replace `csv_name = "output.csv"` with the file name extracted from the URL. For example, for the yellow taxi data, use:
6:    
7:    ```python
8:    url = "https://github.com/DataTalksClub/nyc-tlc-data/releases/download/yellow/yellow_tripdata_2021-01.csv.gz"
9:    csv_name = url.split("/")[-1]
10:    ```
11: 
12: 2. When you use `csv_name` with `pandas.read_csv`, it will work correctly because `pandas.read_csv` can directly read files with the `csv.gz` extension.
13: 
14: Example:
15: 
16: ```python
17: import pandas as pd
18: 
19: url = "https://github.com/DataTalksClub/nyc-tlc-data/releases/download/yellow/yellow_tripdata_2021-01.csv.gz"
20: csv_name = url.split("/")[-1]
21: 
22: data = pd.read_csv(csv_name)
23: ```

FAQ section: Workshop 1 - dlthub
FAQ question: REST API pagination should start at page 1 and stop when the API returns an empty list

Document (the answer, with line numbers):
1: Problem:
2: - Some REST APIs paginate results using a page parameter where valid pages start at 1. Using page=0 can return an empty list, leading to incomplete ingestion.
3: 
4: Best practice:
5: - Start from page=1
6: - Continuously request subsequent pages until the API returns an empty list
7: - Do not rely on page=0 to fetch data; always test the API behaviour manually before implementing pagination logic
8: 
9: Implementation example (Python):
10: ```python
11: import requests
12: 
13: def fetch_all_pages(base_url, start_page=1, per_page=None):
14:     page = start_page
15:     all_items = []
16:     while True:
17:         params = {'page': page}
18:         if per_page is not None:
19:             params['per_page'] = per_page
20:         resp = requests.get(base_url, params=params)
21:         resp.raise_for_status()
22:         data = resp.json()
23:         if not data:
24:             break
25:         all_items.extend(data)
26:         page += 1
27:     return all_items
28: ```
29: 
30: Manual testing steps:
31: - Call the endpoint with page=1 and verify that data is returned.
32: - Call the endpoint with page=0 and verify that it returns an empty list ([]).
33: - Increment the page number (2, 3, ...) until an empty list is returned, confirming ingestion completes when no more data is available.
34: - Add a note to adjust parameter names (e.g., per_page) if the API uses a different paging scheme.
35: 
36: Notes:
37: - If the API uses a different paging convention (e.g., cursor-based, or a different param name), adapt the logic accordingly while preserving the core rule: start at the initial page and stop when there is no data returned.
38: - Consider adding small unit/integration tests that mock API responses to verify this paging behavior in automated tests.

FAQ section: Module 4: Analytics Engineering with dbt
FAQ question: Schema and type errors when ingesting FHV data (timestamps fail to parse, Parquet column type mismatches, NULL handling)

Document (the answer, with line numbers):
1: The FHV 2019 dataset has multiple schema gotchas. The fix depends on which file format you ingested.
2: 
3: **CSV: timestamps fail to parse**
4: 
5: ```
6: Could not parse 'pickup_datetime' as a timestamp
7: ```
8: 
9: Define the timestamp columns as `STRING` in the external table, then cast them in the staging model. This avoids BigQuery rejecting rows with malformed timestamps at load time:
10: 
11: ```sql
12: CREATE OR REPLACE EXTERNAL TABLE `gcp_project.trips_data_all.fhv_tripdata` (
13:   dispatching_base_num STRING,
14:   pickup_datetime STRING,
15:   dropoff_datetime STRING,
16:   PUlocationID STRING,
17:   DOlocationID STRING,
18:   SR_Flag STRING,
19:   Affiliated_base_number STRING
20: )
21: OPTIONS (
22:   format = 'csv',
23:   uris = ['gs://bucket/*.csv']
24: );
25: ```
26: 
27: In your staging model, cast through `TIMESTAMP(CAST(... AS STRING))`:
28: 
29: ```sql
30: SELECT
31:   TIMESTAMP(CAST(pickup_datetime AS STRING)) AS pickup_datetime,
32:   TIMESTAMP(CAST(dropoff_datetime AS STRING)) AS dropoff_datetime,
33:   ...
34: FROM {{ ref('stg_fhv_tripdata') }}
35: ```
36: 
37: To skip type-detection issues entirely, you can also load with `bq load --autodetect --allow_quoted_newlines --source_format=CSV` from a `.csv.gz` file in GCS — see the BigQuery CLI external-table FAQ.
38: 
39: **Parquet: column type mismatch (FLOAT vs INT) or NULL location IDs**
40: 
41: ```
42: Parquet column 'PULocationID' has type INT64 which does not match the target cpp_type DOUBLE
43: Could not parse SR_Flag as Float64
44: ```
45: 
46: Pandas reads integer columns with NULL values as floats by default, which produces a Parquet file with `DOUBLE` columns. BigQuery's external table then conflicts with your declared schema.
47: 
48: Two options:
49: 
50: a) Define the external table schema with `FLOAT64` for the offending location ID columns (matches what Parquet actually has):
51: 
52: ```sql
53: CREATE OR REPLACE EXTERNAL TABLE `dw-bigquery-week-3.trips_data_all.external_tlc_fhv_trips_2019` (
54:   dispatching_base_num STRING,
55:   pickup_datetime TIMESTAMP,
56:   dropoff_datetime TIMESTAMP,
57:   PUlocationID FLOAT64,
58:   DOlocationID FLOAT64,
59:   SR_Flag FLOAT64,
60:   Affiliated_base_number STRING
61: )
62: OPTIONS (
63:   format = 'PARQUET',
64:   uris = ['gs://project/fhv_2019_*.parquet']
65: );
66: ```
67: 
68: b) Fix the Parquet at write time by using pandas' nullable `Int64`:
69: 
70: ```python
71: df['PUlocationID'] = df['PUlocationID'].astype('Int64')
72: df['DOlocationID'] = df['DOlocationID'].astype('Int64')
73: ```
74: 
75: Or coerce the whole DataFrame:
76: 
77: ```python
78: df.fillna(-999999, inplace=True)
79: df = df.convert_dtypes()
80: df = df.replace(-999999, None)
81: ```
82: 
83: This produces a Parquet file with the right INT64 schema and avoids the issue downstream.
84: 
85: **When the column types differ between months**
86: 
87: Some FHV month files have `PUlocationID` as INT, others as FLOAT, leading to:
88: 
89: ```
90: error: Error while reading data: Parquet column 'PUlocationID' has type INT which does not match the target cpp_type DOUBLE
91: ```
92: 
93: The first file BigQuery loads defines the table schema, and subsequent files with a different schema fail. Force consistent types when generating the Parquet (option b above) or load the months that have the same schema in groups.
94: 
95: **"Bad int64 value" on cast in the dbt model**
96: 
97: For `ehail_fee`, `ratecodeid`, `trip_type`, etc. — see the dedicated bad-int64 / parquet-schema FAQ.

FAQ section: Module 5: Data Platforms (Bruin)
FAQ question: Why does my Bruin seed asset fail with a timeout error related to ingestr or duckdb installation?

Document (the answer, with line numbers):
1: Bruin seed assets can fail with a timeout when Bruin dynamically installs the ingestr package and the DuckDB wheel during execution. If the network is slow or unstable, the installer steps may time out, causing the pipeline to fail.
2: 
3: - Bruin uses uv to install required dependencies at run time.
4: - The ingestr package and the DuckDB wheel are downloaded during seed asset execution.
5: - Slow or unreliable network connectivity can cause installation to exceed the timeout.
6: 
7: 1. Increase the HTTP timeout for uv
8: 
9: ```bash
10: export UV_HTTP_TIMEOUT=120
11: ```
12: 
13: 2. Ensure stable network connectivity during seed execution.
14: 
15: 3. For small static lookup tables, replace the seed asset with a SQL asset using a VALUES clause to avoid dynamic dependency installation.
16: 
17: ```sql
18: SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('A'), ('B'), ('C')) AS t(col);
19: ```
20: 
21: - Using SQL VALUES can provide more deterministic local execution when the lookup table is small and static.
22: - If you frequently depend on large non-static datasets, consider pre-bundling or caching dependencies to reduce runtime installation time.

FAQ section: Module 4: Analytics Engineering with dbt
FAQ question: What is the difference between ref() and source() in dbt?

Document (the answer, with line numbers):
1: In dbt, source() and ref() are both used to reference tables, but they serve different purposes in the data pipeline.
2: 
3: source() – Referencing External Source Tables
4: source() is used to reference raw or external tables that are not created by dbt.
5: These tables usually live in a data warehouse such as BigQuery or Snowflake and are defined in a sources.yml file.
6: 
7: Key points:
8: - Used for raw / upstream data
9: - Defined in sources.yml
10: - dbt does not control how the table is created
11: - Enables freshness checks, documentation, and testing
12: 
13: Example:
14: ```sql
15: SELECT *
16: FROM {{ source('raw', 'trips') }}
17: ```
18: 
19: ref() – Referencing dbt Models
20: ref() is used to reference other dbt models (SQL files inside the dbt project).
21: dbt uses ref() to automatically manage model dependencies and execution order.
22: 
23: Key points:
24: - Used for dbt-generated models
25: - Automatically resolves schema and table names
26: - Controls run order and lineage
27: - Enables DAG, documentation, and refactoring safety
28: 
29: Example:
30: ```sql
31: SELECT *
32: FROM {{ ref('stg_trips') }}
33: ```

FAQ section: Module 5: Data Platforms (Bruin)
FAQ question: Why do downstream Bruin assets fail with 'Table does not exist' error even though the upstream ingestion asset succeeded?

Document (the answer, with line numbers):
1: Bruin creates tables inside schemas (for example ingestion, staging, reports). If you reference a table without its schema, DuckDB will not find it and will raise a “Table does not exist” error, even if the upstream ingestion asset ran successfully. Always use schema-qualified names in downstream assets. You can verify existing tables with:
2: 
3: ```bash
4: bruin query -c duckdb-default -q "SELECT table_schema, table_name FROM information_schema.tables;"
5: ```
6: 
7: Example of the pitfall and the fix:
8: 
9: ```
10: -- This will fail if the table was created as ingestion.trips_raw
11: SELECT * FROM trips_raw;
12: 
13: -- Correct:
14: SELECT * FROM ingestion.trips_raw;
15: ```
16: 
17: Notes:
18: - Always reference the fully-qualified table name that the upstream asset created (e.g., ingestion.trips_raw, staging.orders, reports.sales_summary).
19: - If you’re unsure which schema a table lives in, list tables with the command above and inspect the schema column.
20: - Consider using explicit schema qualification in all downstream assets to prevent these errors.

FAQ section: Module 2: Workflow Orchestration
FAQ question: Why does Kestra need access to the Docker socket?

Document (the answer, with line numbers):
1: Kestra runs many tasks inside Docker containers, and Kestra itself is responsible for starting those containers when needed. To do this, Kestra needs access to the host Docker daemon, which is exposed via the Docker socket at /var/run/docker.sock. In the official Docker Compose setup for Kestra, the container runs as root and mounts /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock, because the Docker Compose implementation requires root privileges to access the socket. This configuration is intended for development purposes.

FAQ section: Module 7: Streaming
FAQ question: Why does the tumbling window job run successfully but the PostgreSQL sink table returns no rows when queried?

Document (the answer, with line numbers):
1: Flink streaming jobs emit results only after the window closes. With event-time processing and watermarks, the window will not close until the watermark passes the window end. If you query the PostgreSQL table too early, it may still be empty even though the job is running correctly. Let the job run for a short time so the watermark advances and the window results are written to the sink table.

12: **Missing or out-of-date `typing_extensions`**
13: 
14: ```
15: ImportError: cannot import name 'TypeAliasType' from 'typing_extensions'
16: ```
17: 
18: Upgrade to 4.6+:
19: 
20: ```bash
21: pip install --upgrade typing_extensions
22: ```
23: 
24: **Missing the Postgres driver**
25: 
26: ```
27: ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'psycopg2'
28: ```
29: 
30: Install one of the binary distributions (avoids needing libpq dev headers):
31: 
32: ```bash
33: pip install psycopg2-binary
34: # or, for SQLAlchemy 2.x with psycopg 3:
35: pip install "psycopg[binary]"
36: ```
37: 
38: If `pip install psycopg2` fails with `pg_config not found`, you don't have libpq dev headers installed — use `psycopg2-binary` (or, on Mac, `brew install postgresql`).
39: 
40: **Connection-string dialect mismatch**
41: 
42: `create_engine('postgresql://...')` works with both psycopg2 and psycopg, but to be explicit:
43: 
44: ```python
45: # psycopg2 (most common)
46: "postgresql+psycopg2://root:root@localhost:5432/ny_taxi"
47: 
48: # psycopg (v3)
49: "postgresql+psycopg://root:root@localhost:5432/ny_taxi"
50: ```
51: 
52: If you see `NoSuchModuleError: Can't load plugin: sqlalchemy.dialects:postgresql.psycopg`, your installed psycopg version doesn't match the dialect string — install the matching driver or change the URL prefix.
53: 
54: **`'module' object is not callable`**
55: 
56: You probably did `import sqlalchemy` and then called `sqlalchemy(...)` instead of `sqlalchemy.create_engine(...)`. Fix:
57: 
58: ```python
59: from sqlalchemy import create_engine
60: engine = create_engine("postgresql+psycopg://root:root@localhost:5432/ny_taxi")
61: ```
62: 
63: **Stacked virtual environments**
64: 
65: If you've nested virtualenvs (for example a PyCharm-generated `.venv` inside a project that already had its own venv), imports may resolve from a different env than you think. Cleanest fix: `rm -rf .venv`, create a single venv with `uv venv` (or `python -m venv`), and install dependencies there.

FAQ question: GCP: BQ - Create External Table using Python

Document (the answer, with line numbers):
1: Reference:
2: 
3: [https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/external-data-cloud-storage](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/external-data-cloud-storage)
4: 
5: Solution:
6: 
7: ```python
8: from google.cloud import bigquery
9: 
10: # Set table_id to the ID of the table to create
11: table_id = f"{project_id}.{dataset_name}.{table_name}"
12: 
13: # Construct a BigQuery client object
14: client = bigquery.Client()
15: 
16: # Set the external source format of your table
17: external_source_format = "PARQUET"
18: 
19: # Set the source_uris to point to your data in Google Cloud
20: source_uris = [f'gs://{bucket_name}/{object_key}/*']
21: 
22: # Create ExternalConfig object with external source format
23: external_config = bigquery.ExternalConfig(external_source_format)
24: 
25: # Set source_uris that point to your data in Google Cloud
26: external_config.source_uris = source_uris
27: external_config.autodetect = True
28: 
29: table = bigquery.Table(table_id)
30: 
31: # Set the external data configuration of the table
32: table.external_data_configuration = external_config
33: table = client.create_table(table)  # Make an API request.
34: 
35: print(f'Created table with external source: {table_id}')
36: print(f'Format: {table.external_data_configuration.source_format}')
37: ```

FAQ section: Module 3: Data Warehousing
FAQ question: BigQuery: Datetime columns in Parquet files created from Pandas show up as integer columns in BigQuery

Document (the answer, with line numbers):
1: When writing Parquet files from a Pandas DataFrame, Pandas may emit timestamp columns as integers (epoch milliseconds) by default. When BigQuery loads those files it sees raw `INT64` values and won't auto-promote them to `TIMESTAMP`.
2: 
3: Solution 1: Coerce timestamps when writing the Parquet file
4: 
5: Use PyArrow with `coerce_timestamps='us'` so the file carries proper `TIMESTAMP(MICROS)` logical types:
6: 
7: ```python
8: import pyarrow as pa
9: import pyarrow.parquet as pq
10: 
11: table = pa.Table.from_pandas(df, preserve_index=False)
12: 
13: pq.write_table(
14:     table,
15:     'gs://<bucket>/<path>.parquet',
16:     # Force TIMESTAMP(MICROS) so BigQuery loads the column as TIMESTAMP
17:     coerce_timestamps='us',
18:     filesystem=pa.fs.GcsFileSystem(),
19: )
20: ```
21: 
22: Solution 2: Provide an explicit schema
23: 
24: If you want full control over column types, pass an explicit PyArrow schema instead of relying on inference:
25: 
26: ```python
27: schema = pa.schema([
28:     ('vendor_id', pa.int64()),
29:     ('lpep_pickup_datetime', pa.timestamp('us')),
30:     ('lpep_dropoff_datetime', pa.timestamp('us')),
31:     # ...
32: ])
33: 
34: table = pa.Table.from_pandas(df, schema=schema)
35: ```
36: 
37: Either approach also works inside an orchestrator's data-export task — adapt the `pq.write_table` call to fit your task's signature.

FAQ question: How do I authenticate dbt with BigQuery when service account key creation is disabled and switch to OAuth?

Document (the answer, with line numbers):

FAQ section: Module 1: Postgres, pgAdmin & Python ingestion
FAQ question: Why is my table not being created in PostgreSQL when I submit a job?

Document (the answer, with line numbers):
1: There could be a few reasons for this issue:
2: 
3: - **Race Conditions**: If you're running multiple processes in parallel.
4: 
5: - **Database Connection Issues**: The job might not be connecting to the correct PostgreSQL database, or there could be authentication or permission issues preventing table creation.
6: 
7: - **Missing Table Creation Logic**: The code responsible for creating the table might not be properly included or executed in the job submission process.
8: 
9: As a best practice, it's generally recommended to pre-create tables in PostgreSQL to avoid runtime errors. This ensures the database schema is properly set up before any jobs are executed.
10: 
11: Extra: Use `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` in your code. This will prevent errors if the table already exists and ensure smooth job execution.

4:

18:        build:
19:          context: .
20:          dockerfile: Dockerfile
21:        image: custom-kestra
22:    ```
23:

FAQ section: Module 4: Analytics Engineering with dbt
FAQ question: dbt + BigQuery: "Dataset was not found in location" / region mismatch errors

Document (the answer, with line numbers):
1: This is the single most common dbt+BigQuery problem in the course. The various "404 Not found: Dataset was not found in location X" errors all come down to the same root cause: a region mismatch between
2: 
3: - the source dataset (e.g. `trips_data_all`),
4: - the dbt-managed dev/prod dataset (e.g. `dbt_<initial><lastname>` or `prod`), and
5: - the connection's configured location in dbt Cloud or `profiles.yml`.
6: 
7: BigQuery cannot read and write across regions in a single query, and dbt creates new datasets in whatever location its connection is configured to use. If those don't match your source data's region, you'll see one of:
8: 
9: ```
10: 404 Not found: Dataset <project>:<schema> was not found in location <region>
11: Access Denied: ... or perhaps it does not exist in location <region>
12: ```
13: 
14: 1. Find the location of your source dataset in the BigQuery console (open the dataset → "Details" → "Data location"). Note the exact region string, e.g. `EU`, `US`, `europe-west6`, `us-central1`.
15: 
16: 2. Set dbt's connection location to the same value:
17:    - dbt Cloud: Account settings → Projects → your project → Connection (BigQuery) → Optional Settings → Location.
18:    - dbt Core: in `profiles.yml`, under your target, set `location: <region>`.
19: 
20: 3. If dbt already created datasets in the wrong region, delete those datasets in BigQuery and re-run `dbt build` so they are recreated in the correct region.
21: 
22: 4. For dbt Cloud Production / CI jobs specifically:
23:    - Deploy → Environments → your environment → Settings → Deployment credentials. Confirm "Dataset" matches a dataset that exists in the right region.
24:    - When CI is creating a new schema for each PR, the location is inherited from the connection's location setting (step 2). Make sure that's set to your source region, not the default `US`.
25: 
26: 5. If you genuinely need cross-region data (e.g. source is in `EU` but you want results in `US`), copy or replicate the source dataset into the target region first using BigQuery's dataset-copy feature. Don't try to query across regions.
27: 
28: **In a dbt model**
29: 
30: You can also pin a specific model's location via `config()`:
31: 
32: ```sql
33: {{ config(
34:     materialized='table',
35:     location='EU'
36: ) }}
37: ```
38: 
39: But it's cleaner to fix this once at the connection level than to repeat it in every model.
40: 
41: **Common variants**
42: 
43: - "prod was not found in location EU" → step 2: set connection location to EU, then step 3.
44: - "Access Denied: ... or perhaps it does not exist in location US" → same, plus check the service account has access.
45: - "BigQuery adapter: 404 ... in location europe-west6" → set connection location to `europe-west6` exactly (not `EU`).
46: - A new dataset appears in `US` after a CI run while everything else is in `EU` → step 2 (the connection's location is wrong) and step 4 (CI inherits it).

5: ```sql
6: SELECT [attributes]

9: GROUP BY [grouping attributes]

13: ON [attributes table joining table2] (...)

FAQ section: Workshop 1 - dlthub
FAQ question: What is the difference between rest_api_source({...}) and @dlt.resource in dlt, and when should I use each?

Document (the answer, with line numbers):
1: - `rest_api_source({...})` is declarative: JSON config, less custom code, and faster setup.
2: - `@dlt.resource` is programmatic: a custom Python function, more flexible, and allows custom logic.
3: 
4: When to use `rest_api_source({...})`:
5: - API is simple and consistent
6: - Pagination/params/selectors are standard
7: - You want fast setup with less custom code
8: 
9: When to use `@dlt.resource`:
10: - Response schema is inconsistent or dynamic
11: - You need custom stop/retry/error rules
12: - You need custom preprocessing/validation logic
13: - You need fine-grained behavior for production scenarios
14: 
15: Quick summary:
16: - `rest_api_source({...})` = faster and cleaner for standard APIs
17: - `@dlt.resource` = more flexible for real-world custom APIs
18: 
19: Execution lifecycle is the same for both:
20: - `pipeline.run(...)` -> `extract + normalize + load`

FAQ section: Module 6: Spark
FAQ question: Setting JAVA_HOME with Homebrew on Apple Silicon (M1/M2/M3 Macs)

Document (the answer, with line numbers):
1: Apple Silicon Macs install Homebrew under `/opt/homebrew/` instead of `/usr/local/`. Generic instructions written for Intel Macs won't find the JDK. Set `JAVA_HOME` explicitly in `~/.zshrc` (or `~/.bashrc`):
2: 
3: ```bash
4: brew install openjdk@17
5: 
6: export JAVA_HOME="/opt/homebrew/opt/openjdk@17"
7: export PATH="${JAVA_HOME}/bin:${PATH}"
8: ```
9: 
10: Reload your shell (`source ~/.zshrc` or open a new terminal) and verify:
11: 
12: ```bash
13: which java
14: java --version
15: ```
16: 
17: `which java` should print a path under `/opt/homebrew/...` and `java --version` should show JDK 17.
18: 
19: Spark 4.x supports Java 17 and 21; pick whichever is available via Homebrew (`brew install openjdk@21` works the same way).

FAQ section: Module 1: GCP setup & VM
FAQ question: GCP VM: SSH suddenly stopped working after a restart

Document (the answer, with line numbers):
1: A common cause is the VM running out of disk space, often from accumulated logs, Docker images/volumes, or pipeline artifacts. When the disk fills up, sshd may fail to write its session files and refuse new connections.
2: 
3: To diagnose and recover:
4: 
5: 1. Open a serial console for the VM from the GCP console (Compute Engine → VM details → "Connect to serial console").
6: 2. Check disk usage:
7:    ```bash
8:    df -h
9:    du -sh ~/* /var/log/* 2>/dev/null | sort -h
10:    ```
11: 3. Free up space by clearing unused Docker resources and old logs:
12:    ```bash
13:    docker system prune -af --volumes
14:    sudo journalctl --vacuum-time=7d
15:    ```
16: 4. If your pipeline tool keeps a local storage/log folder (e.g. dlt's `~/.dlt`, dbt's `target/`, Kestra's mounted volumes), prune the oldest content there too.
17: 
18: Once disk space is freed, restart sshd or reboot the VM and SSH access should work again.

FAQ section: Module 7: Streaming
FAQ question: How do I avoid backpressure in a Flink streaming job?

Document (the answer, with line numbers):
1: Backpressure occurs when Flink processes data slower than the upstream source produces it. This causes growing buffers, increased memory usage, and can eventually slow down or crash the job.
2: 
3: How to mitigate it:
4: 
5: - Increase consumer parallelism so more tasks process records in parallel.
6: - Increase the number of partitions on the source topic so the additional Flink consumers actually have separate partitions to read from.
7: - Watch Flink's metrics (the "Backpressure" tab in the Web UI, or the `inputRate`/`outputRate` task metrics) to confirm where the bottleneck is.
8: 
9: Setting parallelism in PyFlink:
10: 
11: ```python
12: env.set_parallelism(4)
13: ```
14: 
15: Increase parallelism gradually and re-check metrics — making it too large just shifts the bottleneck somewhere else (network, sink, etc.).

FAQ section: Module 2: Workflow Orchestration
FAQ question: Kestra: "host.docker.internal" connection failures on Linux

Document (the answer, with line numbers):
1: `host.docker.internal` is a Docker Desktop convenience that resolves to the host machine. On native Linux Docker (and many Linux server setups) it doesn't resolve by default, so Kestra tasks that try to reach Postgres or other services via `host.docker.internal` fail with errors like:
2: 
3: ```
4: The connection attempt failed.
5: could not translate host name "host.docker.internal" to address: Name or service not known
6: ```
7: 
8: You have two options.
9: 
10: **Option 1 (recommended): use the container service name**
11: 
12: If Kestra and Postgres are in the same `docker-compose.yml`, just refer to Postgres by its service name. Replace `host.docker.internal` with the service name (e.g. `postgres_zoomcamp`) in `pluginDefaults`:
13: 
14: ```yaml
15: pluginDefaults:
16:   - type: io.kestra.plugin.jdbc.postgresql
17:     values:
18:       url: jdbc:postgresql://postgres_zoomcamp:5432/postgres-zoomcamp
19:       username: kestra
20:       password: k3str4
21: ```
22: 
23: Apply this in flows like `02_postgres_taxi.yaml` and `2_postgres_taxi_scheduled.yaml`.
24: 
25: **Option 2: add `extra_hosts` so `host.docker.internal` resolves on Linux**
26: 
27: Add an `extra_hosts` entry to the Kestra service in `docker-compose.yml`:
28: 
29: ```yaml
30: services:
31:   kestra:
32:     image: kestra/kestra:latest
33:     extra_hosts:
34:       - "host.docker.internal:host-gateway"
35:     # ...
36: ```

FAQ section: Module 2: Workflow Orchestration
FAQ question: Kestra: how do I authenticate to Google Cloud with a service account?

Document (the answer, with line numbers):
1: Never paste the service account JSON directly into a Kestra flow — it ends up in version control if you push the flow to GitHub. Use Kestra secrets or the KV store instead.
2: 
3: **Option 1: KV store (simplest, recommended for the course)**
4: 
5: 1. Open the Namespaces tab in Kestra and select your namespace (e.g. `zoomcamp`).
6: 2. Go to KV Store → New value.
7: 3. Set the key to `GCP_CREDS` (or whatever name your flow expects), set the type to JSON, and paste the contents of your service account key file.
8: 4. Reference it in your flow's `pluginDefaults`:
9: 
10: ```yaml
11: pluginDefaults:
12:   - type: io.kestra.plugin.gcp
13:     values:
14:       serviceAccount: "{{ kv('GCP_CREDS') }}"
15:       projectId: "{{ kv('GCP_PROJECT_ID') }}"
16: ```
17: 
18: All GCP plugin tasks (BigQuery, GCS, Dataproc, etc.) will pick up the credentials automatically.
19: 
20: **Option 2: Encoded secret (when you can't use KV store)**
21: 
22: 1. Base64-encode the service account JSON and store it in `.env_encoded` (which must be `.gitignore`d):
23: 
24: ```bash
25: base64 service-account.json > .env_encoded
26: ```
27: 
28: 2. Pass the encoded value to Kestra via Docker Compose `environment` and decode it as a Kestra secret. See [Kestra's Google credentials guide](https://kestra.io/docs/how-to-guides/google-credentials#add-service-account-as-a-secret).
29: 
30: 3. Reference in flows with `{{ secret('GCP_SERVICE_ACCOUNT') }}`.
31: 
32: - Always add `.env_encoded` (and any local copy of the JSON key) to `.gitignore`. Base64 is encoding, not encryption — anyone who sees the file can decode it.
33: - To rotate the credential: generate a new key in GCP, re-run the encoding/upload step, and restart Kestra.
34: - Both methods cover all GCP plugins — once configured in `pluginDefaults`, individual tasks (BigQuery, GCS, etc.) inherit the credentials.

FAQ section: Module 3: Data Warehousing
FAQ question: BigQuery: native tables vs external tables — what's the difference and how do I create them?

Document (the answer, with line numbers):
1: A native (regular) table stores data inside BigQuery's managed storage. An external table only stores metadata in BigQuery — the actual data lives in GCS (or S3, Drive). When you query an external table, BigQuery reads the underlying files at query time.
2: 
3: Trade-offs:
4: 
5: - Native: faster queries, partition/cluster support, predictable cost. Uses BigQuery storage.
6: - External: no data duplication, easy to add files via globs. Slower than native, fewer optimizations, query cost depends on bytes scanned in GCS.
7: 
8: **Create an external table from Parquet files in GCS**
9: 
10: ```sql
11: CREATE OR REPLACE EXTERNAL TABLE `your_project.your_dataset.yellow_taxi_external`
12: OPTIONS (
13:   format = 'PARQUET',
14:   uris = ['gs://your-bucket/yellow_tripdata_2024-*.parquet']
15: );
16: ```
17: 
18: The `*` wildcard lets you point at every monthly file at once. Make sure all files have a compatible schema.
19: 
20: **Create a native table from an existing external table**
21: 
22: ```sql
23: CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE `your_project.your_dataset.yellow_taxi`
24: AS
25: SELECT * FROM `your_project.your_dataset.yellow_taxi_external`;
26: ```
27: 
28: This materializes the data into BigQuery storage so subsequent queries are faster and cheaper.
29: 
30: **Can I create an external table directly from a public URL (e.g. nyc.gov)?**
31: 
32: No — BigQuery's external table sources are limited to Cloud Storage, BigTable, and Google Drive. To use data from a public URL, download it to a GCS bucket first (manually, with `gsutil cp`, or via your ingestion pipeline), then point the external table at the bucket.
33: 
34: References:
35: - [External tables](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/external-tables)
36: - [Tables introduction](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/tables-intro)

FAQ section: Module 1: GCP setup & VM
FAQ question: GCP: How do I create a service account key when 'service account key creation is disabled'?

Document (the answer, with line numbers):
1: This error occurs when your organization has a policy that disables service account key creation. You can disable this policy using either the GCP Console or gcloud CLI.
2: 
3: **Option 1: Using GCP Console**
4: 
5: 1. Go to the [IAM dashboard](https://console.cloud.google.com/iam-admin/iam) (IAM & Admin > IAM)
6: 2. Press Ctrl + O and make sure you select your organization
7: 3. Click the "Edit Principal" button (pencil icon) next to your account
8: 4. Search for "Organization Policy Administrator" role, add it and click save
9: 5. On the left sidebar, go to [Organization Policies](https://console.cloud.google.com/iam-admin/orgpolicies/list)
10: 6. Look for the policy named "Disable service account key creation" that is active and select it
11: 7. Click on "Manage policy" then click on the drop down that says "Enforced", set it to "Off"
12: 8. Click "Done" and then the blue "Set policy" button
13: 
14: **Option 2: Using gcloud CLI**
15: 
16: ```bash
17: # Get your organization ID
18: gcloud organizations list
19: 
20: # Get your account email
21: gcloud auth list
22: 
23: # Add policy admin role if needed
24: gcloud organizations add-iam-policy-binding <ORGANIZATION_ID> \
25:   --member="user:<YOUR_ACCOUNT_EMAIL>" \
26:   --role="roles/orgpolicy.policyAdmin"
27: 
28: # Delete the policy
29: gcloud org-policies delete iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation \
30:   --organization=<ORGANIZATION_ID>
31: ```
32: 
33: Reference: [GCP Organization Policies](https://cloud.google.com/resource-manager/docs/secure-by-default-organizations#disable_organization_policies)

FAQ section: Module 3: Data Warehousing
FAQ question: How to obtain the DDL of a table in BigQuery?

Document (the answer, with line numbers):
1: To reproduce a BigQuery table's schema and data layout, you can query the INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TABLES to retrieve the DDL needed to recreate the table.
2: 
3: **For a normal (native) table in a dataset**
4: 
5: ```sql
6: SELECT table_name, ddl
7: FROM zoomcamp.INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TABLES
8: WHERE table_name = 'yellow_tripdata_parquet';
9: ```
10: 
11: The result is the `CREATE TABLE` statement needed to recreate the table, e.g.:
12: 
13: ```sql
14: CREATE TABLE `zoomcamp-ingenieria-datos.zoomcamp.yellow_tripdata_parquet`
15: (
16:     VendorID INT64,
17:     tpep_pickup_datetime TIMESTAMP,
18:     tpep_dropoff_datetime TIMESTAMP,
19:     passenger_count INT64,
20:     trip_distance FLOAT64,
21:     RatecodeID INT64,
22:     store_and_fwd_flag STRING,
23:     PULocationID INT64,
24:     DOLocationID INT64,
25:     payment_type INT64,
26:     fare_amount FLOAT64,
27:     extra FLOAT64,
28:     mta_tax FLOAT64,
29:     tip_amount FLOAT64,
30:     tolls_amount FLOAT64,
31:     improvement_surcharge FLOAT64,
32:     total_amount FLOAT64,
33:     congestion_surcharge FLOAT64,
34:     Airport_fee FLOAT64
35: );
36: ```
37: 
38: **For an external table**
39: 
40: ```sql
41: SELECT table_name, ddl
42: FROM zoomcamp.INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TABLES
43: WHERE table_name = 'yellow_tripdata_parquet_ext';
44: ```
45: 
46: The result would contain the DDL including the path of the external files, e.g.:
47: 
48: ```sql
49: CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE `zoomcamp-ingenieria-datos.zoomcamp.yellow_tripdata_parquet_ext`
50: OPTIONS(
51:     format="PARQUET",
52:     uris=["gs://newyork-taxi/yellow_tripdata_*.parquet"]
53: );
54: ```
55: 
56: Notes
57: - This method works for both native and external tables. The exact path and URIs will depend on your dataset.
58: - For more details, see the BigQuery information_schema-tables documentation.

FAQ section: Module 1: Docker
FAQ question: docker compose: "could not translate host name pgdatabase / pg-database to address" — hostname does not resolve

Document (the answer, with line numbers):
1: This error means your container is looking for another service by name on a Docker network, but they aren't on the same network. Common variants:
2: 
3: ```
4: sqlalchemy.exc.OperationalError: could not translate host name "pgdatabase" to address: Name or service not known
5: Unable to connect to server: could not translate host name 'pg-database' to address: Name does not resolve
6: network <hash> not found
7: ```
8: 
9: **What's happening**
10: 
11: Docker network DNS only resolves service names within the same network. Two reasons it might fail:
12: 
13: 1. The ingestion container was started with `--network <name>` but `<name>` doesn't match the network compose actually created. By default, `docker compose` creates a network named after the project directory plus `_default` (e.g. `2docker_default`).
14: 
15: 2. Your ingestion script is hardcoded to use a host name like `pgdatabase`, but the compose service is actually called `pgdatabase-1`, or you're running the script outside Docker entirely.
16: 
17: 1. List networks and confirm the actual name compose created:
18: 
19:    ```bash
20:    docker network ls
21:    ```
22: 
23:    Pass that exact name when running the ingestion container:
24: 
25:    ```bash
26:    docker run --network=<actual_network_name> taxi_ingest:v001 ...
27:    ```
28: 
29:    Or pin the network name in your `docker-compose.yml` so it doesn't depend on the directory name:
30: 
31:    ```yaml
32:    networks:
33:      pg-network:
34:        name: pg-network
35:    ```
36: 
37: 2. Make the host name in your script match the compose service name. If your service is called `pgdatabase`, the script should use `--pg_host=pgdatabase` (when running inside Docker) or `--pg_host=localhost` (when running on the host).
38: 
39: 3. Avoid hostnames with dashes when possible — `pgdatabase` is more reliable than `pg-database` across some networks/DNS configs.
40: 
41: 4. If `docker network ls` shows a stale network from a previous run, prune it: `docker network prune` (after stopping the relevant containers).
42: 
43: **Working compose snippet**
44: 
45: ```yaml
46: services:
47:   pgdatabase:
48:     image: postgres:16
49:     environment:
50:       POSTGRES_USER: root
51:       POSTGRES_PASSWORD: root
52:       POSTGRES_DB: ny_taxi
53:     volumes:
54:       - "pg-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data"
55:     ports:
56:       - "5432:5432"
57:     networks:
58:       - pg-network
59: 
60:   pgadmin:
61:     image: dpage/pgadmin4
62:     environment:
63:       PGADMIN_DEFAULT_EMAIL: admin@admin.com
64:       PGADMIN_DEFAULT_PASSWORD: root
65:     ports:
66:       - "8080:80"
67:     networks:
68:       - pg-network
69: 
70: networks:
71:   pg-network:
72:     name: pg-network
73: 
74: volumes:
75:   pg-data:
76: ```

FAQ section: Module 6: Spark
FAQ question: TypeError when using spark.createDataFrame function on a pandas df

Document (the answer, with line numbers):
1: **Error:**
2: 
3: ```python
4: spark.createDataFrame(df_pandas).schema
5: 
6: TypeError: field Affiliated_base_number: Can not merge type <class 'pyspark.sql.types.StringType'> and <class 'pyspark.sql.types.DoubleType'>
7: ```
8: 
9: **Solution:**
10: 
11: - **Reason:**
12:   - The `Affiliated_base_number` field is a mix of letters and numbers, so it cannot be set to `DoubleType`. The suitable type would be `StringType`. Spark's `inferSchema` is more accurate than Pandas' infer type method in this case. Set `inferSchema` to `true` when reading the CSV to prevent data removal.
13: 
14: - **Implementation:**
15:   
16:   ```python
17:   df = spark.read \
18:     .options(
19:       header = "true", \
20:       inferSchema = "true"
21:     ) \
22:     .csv('path/to/your/csv/file/')
23:   ````
24: 
25: - **Alternative Solution:**
26:   
27:   - **Problem:** Some rows in `affiliated_base_number` are null, and therefore are assigned the datatype `String`, which cannot be converted to `Double`.
28:   - **Solution:** Only take rows from the pandas df that are not null in the 'Affiliated_base_number' column before converting it to a PySpark DataFrame.
29: 
30:   ```python
31:   # Only take rows that have no null values
32:   pandas_df = pandas_df[pandas_df.notnull().all(1)]
33:   ```

FAQ section: Module 1: Docker
FAQ question: What's the difference between -i and -t in docker run -it?

Document (the answer, with line numbers):
1: ```markdown
2: ## Difference between -i and -t in docker run (-it)
3: 
4: When running containers interactively, Docker provides two commonly used flags:
5: 
6: - `-i` (interactive): keeps the container’s STDIN open, even if it is not attached to a terminal. This allows you to send input to the process inside the container.
7:   Example:
8:   ```bash
9:   echo "print(2+2)" | docker run -i python
10:   ```
11: 
12: - `-t` (tty): allocates a pseudo-terminal (TTY) for the container. This provides proper terminal formatting (line breaks, colors, prompts).
13:   Example:
14:   ```bash
15:   docker run -t ubuntu date
16:   ```
17: 
18: Using both flags together (`-it`) gives you both an open input stream and a real terminal interface. This is typically what you want for an interactive shell session:
19:   
20:   ```bash
21:   docker run -it ubuntu bash
22:   ```
23: 
24: In short:
25: - `-i` = keep STDIN open
26: - `-t` = allocate a TTY
27: - `-it` = both, for interactive shells
28: ```

FAQ section: Module 7: Streaming
FAQ question: How do you manually manage offsets in a Kafka consumer?

Document (the answer, with line numbers):
1: Kafka allows you to manually control when message offsets are committed. This is useful when you want to **commit offsets only after successful message processing**, ensuring reliable processing.
2: 
3: **Step 1: Disable Auto Commit**
4: 
5: ```python
6: consumer = KafkaConsumer(
7:     'taxi-trips',
8:     bootstrap_servers=['localhost:9092'],
9:     enable_auto_commit=False  # Manual commit
10: )
11: ```
12: 
13: Setting `enable_auto_commit=False` prevents Kafka from automatically committing offsets.
14: 
15: **Step 2: Process Messages and Commit Manually**
16: 
17: ```python
18: for message in consumer:
19:     try:
20:         # Process the message
21:         process_trip(message.value)
22:         # Commit offset after successful processing
23:         consumer.commit()
24:     except Exception as e:
25:         print(f"Error: {e}")
26:         # Do not commit on failure → message will be reprocessed
27: ```
28: 
29: Offsets are committed **only after** the message is successfully processed. If an error occurs, the offset is not committed, so the message can be consumed again.

FAQ section: Environment & Setup
FAQ question: How to troubleshoot issues and ask good questions

Document (the answer, with line numbers):
1: **Try to solve it yourself first**
2: 
3: - Read the error message carefully — it usually includes a line number, a stack trace, and a description of what went wrong.
4: - Search the message: copy the most specific part of the error (not the whole stack trace) into Google. The format `<tool> <error message>` works well, e.g. `pgcli error column c.relhasoids does not exist`.
5: - Check the official documentation of the tool you're using.
6: - Use Ctrl+F in this FAQ and in Slack channel pinned messages.
7: - Restart the process / container / shell / VM and try once more — many transient errors resolve this way.
8: - If you suspect the install is broken, uninstall first, then reinstall. Reinstalling on top of a broken install rarely helps.
9: 
10: **Asking for help in Slack / forums**
11: 
12: When the troubleshooting steps don't help and you need another pair of eyes, include enough info that someone can actually help without going back and forth:
13: 
14: - Operating system and version (e.g. Windows 11 + WSL Ubuntu 24.04, Mac M2, Linux Ubuntu 22.04).
15: - Which lesson / video you're following, and which command failed.
16: - The exact command and the exact error — paste both as text inside triple-backtick code blocks. Don't paste screenshots of text.
17: - What you've already tried. If you skip this, helpers' first suggestions will be the things you already tried.
18: - Stay in one thread. Reply to your own question; don't open a new post for a follow-up.
19: 
20: If the same problem recurs, post in the same thread with what changed in your environment since last time.
21: 
22: **Help others by contributing back**
23: 
24: If your problem isn't yet covered in this FAQ, consider [opening a PR](https://github.com/DataTalksClub/faq) so the next student doesn't have to debug it from scratch.

FAQ section: Module 3: Data Warehousing
FAQ question: GCP BQ - Tip: Using Cloud Function to read csv.gz files from github directly to BigQuery in Google Cloud:

Document (the answer, with line numbers):
1: There are multiple benefits of using Cloud Functions to automate tasks in Google Cloud.
2: 
3: Use the following Cloud Function Python script to load files directly into BigQuery. Set your project ID, dataset ID, and table ID accordingly.
4: 
5: ```python
6: import tempfile
7: import requests
8: import logging
9: from google.cloud import bigquery
10: 
11: def hello_world(request):
12:     # table_id = <project_id.dataset_id.table_id>
13:     table_id = 'de-zoomcap-project.dezoomcamp.fhv-2019'
14: 
15:     # Create a new BigQuery client
16:     client = bigquery.Client()
17: 
18:     for month in range(4, 13):
19:         # Define the schema for the data in the CSV.gz files
20:         url = 'https://github.com/DataTalksClub/nyc-tlc-data/releases/download/fhv/fhv_tripdata_2019-{:02d}.csv.gz'.format(month)
21: 
22:         # Download the CSV.gz file from Github
23:         response = requests.get(url)
24: 
25:         # Create new table if loading first month data else append
26:         write_disposition_string = "WRITE_APPEND" if month > 1 else "WRITE_TRUNCATE"
27: 
28:         # Defining LoadJobConfig with schema of table to prevent it from changing with every table
29:         job_config = bigquery.LoadJobConfig(
30:             schema=[
31:                 bigquery.SchemaField("dispatching_base_num", "STRING"),
32:                 bigquery.SchemaField("pickup_datetime", "TIMESTAMP"),
33:                 bigquery.SchemaField("dropOff_datetime", "TIMESTAMP"),
34:                 bigquery.SchemaField("PUlocationID", "STRING"),
35:                 bigquery.SchemaField("DOlocationID", "STRING"),
36:                 bigquery.SchemaField("SR_Flag", "STRING"),
37:                 bigquery.SchemaField("Affiliated_base_number", "STRING"),
38:             ],
39:             skip_leading_rows=1,
40:             write_disposition=write_disposition_string,
41:             autodetect=True,
42:             source_format="CSV",
43:         )
44: 
45:         # Load the data into BigQuery
46:         # Create a temporary file to prevent the exception: AttributeError: 'bytes' object has no attribute 'tell'
47:         with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile() as f:
48:             f.write(response.content)
49:             f.seek(0)
50: 
51:             job = client.load_table_from_file(
52:                 f,
53:                 table_id,
54:                 location="US",
55:                 job_config=job_config,
56:             )
57: 
58:             job.result()
59: 
60:         logging.info("Data for month %d successfully loaded into table %s.", month, table_id)
61: 
62:     return 'Data loaded into table {}.'.format(table_id)
63: ```

FAQ section: Workshop 1 - dlthub
FAQ question: Why might some API response fields be missing after a dlt pipeline run, and how can I fix it?

Document (the answer, with line numbers):
1: Root cause:
2: - dlt infers column types from actual data in the current load. If a column contains only NULL values in that load, dlt cannot infer its type and the column will not be materialized in the destination table.
3: 
4: Fixes:
5: 1) Provide explicit type hints using the columns argument in the @dlt.resource decorator.
6: 
7: Example:
8: ```python
9: @dlt.resource(columns={
10:     "rate_code": "STRING",
11:     "mta_tax": "FLOAT64"
12: })
13: def api_records():
14:     # your data loading logic here
15:     return fetch_api()
16: ```
17: 
18: 2) Ensure at least one non-null value exists for that column during ingestion.
19:    - If possible, modify the API payload or add a preprocessing step to emit a non-null value for the field (e.g., default values).
20:    - Example pre-processing (in Python):
21: ```python
22: def normalize(record):
23:     if record.get("rate_code") is None:
24:         record["rate_code"] = "UNKNOWN"
25:     if record.get("mta_tax") is None:
26:         record["mta_tax"] = 0.0
27:     return record
28: ```
29: 
30: After applying either fix, re-run the pipeline. The destination table will materialize the specified columns with the defined types.
31: 
32: Tips:
33: - Prefer explicit type hints when you know which fields to expect, especially for optional or nullable fields.
34: - If you cannot guarantee non-null values, always provide the explicit `columns` mapping to avoid missing columns.

FAQ question: How do I manage security and access control in a BigQuery data warehouse?

Document (the answer, with line numbers):
1: BigQuery uses Identity and Access Management (IAM) to control who can view, query, or modify datasets and tables. You can assign roles at the project, dataset, or table level depending on how granular you want permissions to be.
2: 
3: - Common roles:
4: - BigQuery Data Viewer → Read-only access to datasets and tables.
5: - BigQuery Data Editor → Can query and modify data.
6: - BigQuery Admin → Full control, including managing datasets, tables, and jobs.
7: 
8: - Best practices:
9: - Apply the principle of least privilege (give users only the access they need).
10: - Use authorized views to share query results without exposing the underlying raw data.
11: - Enable column-level security if only certain fields should be visible to specific users.
12: - Audit usage with INFORMATION_SCHEMA views to track who ran queries and how much data was processed.
13: 
14: This ensures that your BigQuery data warehouse remains secure while still enabling collaboration across teams.

FAQ section: Module 1: Docker
FAQ question: pgAdmin: persist server / connection settings across container restarts

Document (the answer, with line numbers):
1: By default, the `dpage/pgadmin4` image stores its config (registered servers, query history, etc.) inside the container — so it's lost every time you `docker compose down`.
2: 
3: To persist it, mount `/var/lib/pgadmin` to a Docker volume. Use a named volume rather than a host-bind, because pgAdmin runs as user 5050 and host permissions tend to fight you:
4: 
5: ```yaml
6: services:
7:   pgadmin:
8:     image: dpage/pgadmin4
9:     environment:
10:       - PGADMIN_DEFAULT_EMAIL=admin@admin.com
11:       - PGADMIN_DEFAULT_PASSWORD=root
12:     volumes:
13:       - "pgadmin-data:/var/lib/pgadmin"
14:     ports:
15:       - "8080:80"
16: 
17: volumes:
18:   pgadmin-data:
19: ```
20: 
21: After this, your pgAdmin servers and dashboards survive `docker compose down` and `docker compose up`.
22: 
23: **If you really want a host-bind mount**
24: 
25: You'll need to fix permissions before mounting. pgAdmin's container user is 5050:
26: 
27: ```bash
28: mkdir -p ./pgadmin_data
29: sudo chown -R 5050:5050 ./pgadmin_data
30: ```
31: 
32: Then:
33: 
34: ```yaml
35: volumes:
36:   - "./pgadmin_data:/var/lib/pgadmin"
37: ```
38: 
39: If you skip the chown step, pgAdmin will fail to start with a permission error.
40: 
41: **On GCP / cloud VMs**
42: 
43: Same approach works — use a named volume rather than host-bind to avoid filesystem permission quirks on the cloud disk.

FAQ section: Module 6: Spark
FAQ question: How can I calculate the duration between two Spark timestamp columns in hours (e.g., tpep_pickup_datetime and tpep_dropoff_datetime)?

Document (the answer, with line numbers):
1: You can compute the duration in hours between two Spark timestamp columns in several ways. Choose the approach that best fits your workflow:
2: 
3: - Using unix_timestamp (per-row hours as a floating-point value):
4: ````python
5: from pyspark.sql import functions as F
6: 
7: trip_duration_hours = (
8:     F.unix_timestamp("tpep_dropoff_datetime") -
9:     F.unix_timestamp("tpep_pickup_datetime")
10: ) / 3600
11: ````
12: This yields the duration in hours for each row as a numeric value.
13: 
14: - Using datediff (hours approximation via days):
15: ````python
16: from pyspark.sql import functions as F
17: 
18: # difference in days, then multiply by 24 to get hours
19: hours = F.datediff("tpep_dropoff_datetime", "tpep_pickup_datetime") * 24
20: ````
21: Note that datediff returns whole days; if you need sub-day precision, prefer the unix_timestamp method above or compute seconds directly.
22: 
23: - Working with Python timedelta after collecting (Python-side calculation):
24: ````python
25: # after collecting to Python (e.g., with toPandas or collect):
26: # delta is a Python datetime.timedelta object between dropoff and pickup
27: hours = delta.total_seconds() / 3600
28: ````
29: 
30: Each approach has trade-offs:
31: - unix_timestamp gives per-row exact hours including minutes and seconds.
32: - datediff provides a quick day-based delta (multiplying by 24 to get hours) but loses sub-day precision.
33: - Python-side timedelta is useful when you're operating outside Spark/after collecting, but it requires moving data to the driver.

4:   1) In Looker Studio, click Create > Data Source.

13: 
14: Notes:
15: - You may want to create views in BigQuery to simplify the data schema for BI tools.
16: - For Tableau, consider using extracts if you are working with large datasets or need offline access.
17: - Ensure proper IAM permissions (BigQuery Data Viewer or Editor) for the service account or user used by the BI tool.

FAQ question: GitHub Codespaces: what uses up memory and storage?

FAQ section: Environment & Setup
FAQ question: VMs: What do I do if my VM runs out of space?

Document (the answer, with line numbers):
1: - Delete intermediate data you saved on the VM during ETLs (raw extracts, parquet outputs you've already pushed elsewhere, downloaded archives).
2: - Kill processes still holding deleted files (their disk space isn't reclaimed until the process exits — `lsof | grep deleted` shows them).
3: - Install `ncdu` (`sudo apt install ncdu`) and use it to walk the filesystem visually:
4:   ```bash
5:   sudo ncdu /
6:   ```
7: - Common culprits: Docker images and volumes (`docker system prune -af --volumes`), pipeline working/cache directories, and old logs (`sudo journalctl --vacuum-time=7d`).
8: - If a pipeline tool's cache keeps regrowing (e.g. orchestrator working dir, dbt `target/`, dlt staging), consider disabling caching or pruning it on a schedule rather than only when the disk fills.

FAQ section: Module 1: Postgres, pgAdmin & Python ingestion
FAQ question: pgcli: PermissionError: [Errno 13] Permission denied: '~/.config/pgcli'

Document (the answer, with line numbers):
1: ```
2: PermissionError: [Errno 13] Permission denied: '/Users/<you>/.config/pgcli'
3: ```
4: 
5: This means pgcli can't write its config dir. Two common causes.
6: 
7: **Cause 1: someone ran pgcli with sudo earlier**
8: 
9: Running `sudo pgcli ...` once creates `~/.config/pgcli` owned by root. Subsequent runs as your normal user can't write there. Fix the ownership:
10: 
11: ```bash
12: sudo chown -R "$USER" ~/.config/pgcli
13: ```
14: 
15: Going forward, install and run pgcli without `sudo` — install it into a project venv (recommended) or `pip install --user pgcli` so you don't need root.
16: 
17: **Cause 2: pgcli installed into a system Python you can't write to**
18: 
19: Install pgcli into an isolated environment instead. Recommended path is `uv`:
20: 
21: ```bash
22: uv add pgcli "psycopg[binary]"
23: uv run pgcli -h localhost -p 5432 -u root -d ny_taxi
24: ```
25: 
26: Or with a plain `venv`:
27: 
28: ```bash
29: python3 -m venv .venv
30: source .venv/bin/activate
31: pip install pgcli "psycopg[binary]"
32: ```
33: 
34: Either way, run pgcli from inside the activated environment (or via `uv run pgcli`) — never with `sudo`.

FAQ section: Module 3: Data Warehousing
FAQ question: GCP BQ: How to handle type error from BigQuery and Parquet data?

Document (the answer, with line numbers):
1: When injecting data into GCS using Pandas, some datasets might have missing values in the `DOlocationID` and `PUlocationID` columns. By default, Pandas will cast these columns as `float`, leading to inconsistent data types between the Parquet files in GCS and the schema defined in BigQuery. You might encounter the following error:
2: 
3: ```bash
4: error: Error while reading table: trips_data_all.external_fhv_tripdata, error message: Parquet column 'DOlocationID' has type INT64 which does not match the target cpp_type DOUBLE.
5: ```
6: 
7: Fix the data type issue in the data pipeline:
8: 
9: 1. Before injecting data into GCS, use `astype` and `Int64` (which is different from `int64` and accepts both missing values and integers) to cast the columns.
10: 
11:     Example:
12:     ```python
13:     df["PUlocationID"] = df.PUlocationID.astype("Int64")
14:     df["DOlocationID"] = df.DOlocationID.astype("Int64")
15:     ```
16: 
17: 2. It is best to define the data type of all the columns in the Transformation section of the ETL pipeline before loading to BigQuery.

FAQ question: Can I keep my dbt project in a subfolder of my GitHub repo (instead of the root)?

Document (the answer, with line numbers):
1: Yes. The trick is to leave `dbt_project.yml` at the root of the repo and prefix every path inside it with your subfolder.
2: 
3: For example, to keep all the dbt files in a `Week_4/` folder of the repo:
4: 
5: 1. Keep `dbt_project.yml` in the root of your repo. Edit it so every path is prefixed with your subfolder:
6: 
7:    ```yaml
8:    model-paths: ["Week_4/models"]
9:    analysis-paths: ["Week_4/analyses"]
10:    test-paths: ["Week_4/tests"]
11:    seed-paths: ["Week_4/seeds"]
12:    macro-paths: ["Week_4/macros"]
13:    snapshot-paths: ["Week_4/snapshots"]
14:    target-path: "Week_4/target"
15:    clean-targets:
16:      - "Week_4/target"
17:      - "Week_4/dbt_packages"
18:    ```
19: 
20: 2. Save `dbt_project.yml`.
21: 3. Review your `.gitignore` for any dbt-related entries and update paths if needed.
22: 4. Delete the duplicate dbt files/folders that dbt initially created in the root of your repo — they aren't used now that paths are pointed at the subfolder. (The `target/` folder may re-appear when you run dbt commands; that's fine.)
23: 5. If there's an older copy of `dbt_project.yml` inside the subfolder, delete it so you don't edit the wrong one by accident.
24: 6. Test-run dbt commands from the subfolder to confirm everything works.

FAQ section: Module 1: Docker
FAQ question: docker compose: installation problems (binary not found, exec format error, credentials error, dial unix /var/run/docker.sock)

Document (the answer, with line numbers):
1: Most "docker-compose" installation problems on Linux/WSL fall into a small handful of categories.
2: 
3: **"docker-compose: command not found" / "still not available"**
4: 
5: The downloaded file from the docker/compose releases page has a long platform-suffixed name like `docker-compose-linux-x86_64`. Rename it and put it on your `PATH`:
6: 
7: ```bash
8: sudo mv docker-compose-linux-x86_64 /usr/local/bin/docker-compose
9: sudo chmod +x /usr/local/bin/docker-compose
10: ```
11: 
12: Modern Docker (20.10+) ships compose v2 as `docker compose` (with a space). If you have a recent Docker install, you may not need a separate `docker-compose` binary at all — just use `docker compose up`.
13: 
14: **Picking the right binary for your platform**
15: 
16: Use `uname` to determine which file to download:
17: 
18: ```bash
19: uname -s   # operating system, usually 'Linux'
20: uname -m   # architecture, e.g. 'x86_64' or 'aarch64'
21: ```
22: 
23: Then download the matching release, e.g.:
24: 
25: ```bash
26: sudo curl -L "https://github.com/docker/compose/releases/latest/download/docker-compose-$(uname -s)-$(uname -m)" \
27:   -o /usr/local/bin/docker-compose
28: sudo chmod +x /usr/local/bin/docker-compose
29: ```
30: 
31: Pin a specific release if you need reproducibility (substitute `latest/download` with `download/<version>`).
32: 
33: **"cannot execute binary file: Exec format error"**
34: 
35: The architecture doesn't match. ARM64 machines (Apple Silicon, ARM Linux, some VMs) need the `aarch64` binary, not `x86_64`. Re-download with `uname -m` substituted correctly.
36: 
37: **"error getting credentials" / "docker-credential-desktop not found"**
38: 
39: Docker is looking for a credential helper that isn't installed. Two fixes:
40: 
41: ```bash
42: # Quick: install pass (resolves it on most Linux distros)
43: sudo apt install pass
44: ```
45: 
46: Or edit `~/.docker/config.json` and rename `credsStore` to `credStore` (the helper-less default), or remove the line entirely.
47: 
48: **"dial unix /var/run/docker.sock: connect: permission denied"**
49: 
50: Your user isn't in the `docker` group. Add it:
51: 
52: ```bash
53: sudo groupadd docker
54: sudo usermod -aG docker $USER
55: # log out and back in for the group change to apply
56: ```

FAQ section: Module 6: Spark
FAQ question: Compression Error: zcat output is gibberish, seems like still compressed

Document (the answer, with line numbers):
1: In the code along from Video 5.3.3, Alexey downloads the CSV files from the NYT website and gzips them in their bash script. Currently (2023), if we download the data from the GH course repo, it is already zipped as `csv.gz` files. Following the video exactly would zip them again, leading to gibberish output when using `zcat`, as it only unzips the file once.
2: 
3: **Solution:** Do not gzip the files downloaded from the course repo. Simply use `wget` to download and save them as `csv.gz` files. Then the `zcat` command and the `showSchema` command will work correctly.
4: 
5: ```bash
6: URL="${URL_PREFIX}/${TAXI_TYPE}/${TAXI_TYPE}_tripdata_${YEAR}-${FMONTH}.csv.gz"
7: 
8: LOCAL_PREFIX="data/raw/${TAXI_TYPE}/${YEAR}/${FMONTH}"
9: 
10: LOCAL_FILE="${TAXI_TYPE}_tripdata_${YEAR}_${FMONTH}.csv.gz"
11: 
12: LOCAL_PATH="${LOCAL_PREFIX}/${LOCAL_FILE}"
13: 
14: echo "downloading ${URL} to ${LOCAL_PATH}"
15: 
16: mkdir -p ${LOCAL_PREFIX}
17: 
18: wget ${URL} -O ${LOCAL_PATH}
19: 
20: echo "compressing ${LOCAL_PATH}"
21: 
22: # gzip ${LOCAL_PATH} <- uncomment this line
23: ```

FAQ section: Module 1: Postgres, pgAdmin & Python ingestion
FAQ question: pgcli / Postgres: troubleshooting connection failures (FATAL: password auth, role does not exist, database does not exist, connection refused, port in use)

Document (the answer, with line numbers):
1: The various Postgres connection errors students hit in week 1 almost always trace back to one of three problems. Before changing anything, identify which:
2: 
3: ```
4: connection failed: connection to server at "localhost" port 5432 failed: Connection refused
5: FATAL: password authentication failed for user "root"
6: FATAL: role "root" does not exist
7: FATAL: database "ny_taxi" does not exist
8: psycopg2.OperationalError: connection to server at "localhost" (::1), port 5432 failed
9: ```
10: 
11: **Step 1: confirm the right Postgres is reachable**
12: 
13: Run:
14: 
15: ```bash
16: docker ps
17: ```
18: 
19: You should see the `postgres:13` (or `postgres:16`/`postgres:18`) container with port mapping `0.0.0.0:5432->5432/tcp`. If not, start it:
20: 
21: ```bash
22: docker compose up -d
23: # or, for the standalone docker run:
24: docker run -it -e POSTGRES_USER=root -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=root -e POSTGRES_DB=ny_taxi \
25:   -v ny_taxi_postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data -p 5432:5432 postgres:16
26: ```
27: 
28: **Step 2: check whether port 5432 is already taken on your host**
29: 
30: A locally installed Postgres ("Postgres.app", `apt install postgresql`, the Windows installer, the Mac Homebrew formula) often listens on 5432. When you map the Docker container to the same port, the connection silently goes to the wrong instance — which is usually the source of "FATAL: password authentication failed for user root" or "role root does not exist" (the local install doesn't know about the `root` user).
31: 
32: Linux/Mac:
33: 
34: ```bash
35: sudo lsof -i :5432
36: ```
37: 
38: Windows: open Services (`services.msc`) and look for any `postgresql-x64-XX` service.
39: 
40: You have two options:
41: 
42: - Stop the local Postgres:
43:   - Linux: `sudo service postgresql stop`
44:   - Mac (Homebrew): `launchctl unload -w ~/Library/LaunchAgents/homebrew.mxcl.postgresql.plist`
45:   - Windows: stop the `postgresql-x64-XX` service in Services.
46: 
47: - Or change the Docker mapping to a different host port and connect to that port:
48: 
49:   ```bash
50:   -p 5433:5432
51:   # then
52:   pgcli -h localhost -p 5433 -u root -d ny_taxi
53:   ```
54: 
55: **Step 3: match host names between the script and the runtime**
56: 
57: If the connection error mentions a host name like `pgdatabase` or `pg-database` and says "could not translate host name", you are running an ingestion script that points at a Docker service name from outside the Docker network. Pick one:
58: 
59: - Run the script from inside the same Docker network and use the service name (`pgdatabase`).
60: - Run the script from your host machine and use `localhost` (or `127.0.0.1`).
61: 
62: For the Dockerized ingestion job the course shows, both the container and the Postgres container must share a Docker network — `--network=pg-network` on `docker run`, or the implicit network in `docker compose`.
63: 
64: **Step 4: persistent data corruption / "database ny_taxi does not exist"**
65: 
66: If the database existed before but the `FATAL: database ny_taxi does not exist` error appears now, your Postgres container probably started with an empty data directory. Two common reasons:
67: 
68: - The volume mount path is wrong, so a new empty data dir is being initialised every time.
69: - Volumes were pruned (e.g. `docker compose down -v`).
70: 
71: Either restore data from backup, or wipe the volume and re-ingest:
72: 
73: ```bash
74: docker compose down -v
75: docker compose up -d
76: # then re-run the ingestion script
77: ```
78: 
79: **Step 5: client-side issues (pgcli specifically)**
80: 
81: If pgcli prints `ImportError: no pq wrapper available`, it can't find `libpq` — install the binary psycopg:
82: 
83: ```bash
84: uv add "psycopg[binary]"
85: # or
86: pip install "psycopg[binary]"
87: ```
88: 
89: If pgcli appears to hang at the password prompt on Windows Git Bash, prefix it with `winpty`:
90: 
91: ```bash
92: winpty pgcli -h localhost -p 5432 -u root -d ny_taxi
93: ```
94: 
95: Or use Windows Terminal / VS Code's integrated terminal instead of Git Bash.
96: 
97: **Quick reference**
98: 
99: - `Connection refused` → Postgres isn't running, or it's on a different port. Check `docker ps`.
100: - `FATAL: password authentication failed for user "root"` → almost always a port collision with a locally-installed Postgres.
101: - `FATAL: role "root" does not exist` → same as above (local install doesn't have a `root` user).
102: - `FATAL: database "ny_taxi" does not exist` → Postgres init didn't run, or the volume is empty.
103: - `could not translate host name "pgdatabase"` → wrong host name for where you're connecting from (host vs container network).

5: - Appending instead of replacing during reload
6: - Partial failed loads
7: 
8: How to verify:
9: 
10: - Run a range check:
11: 
12: ```sql
13: SELECT
14:   MIN(lpep_pickup_datetime),
15:   MAX(lpep_pickup_datetime)
16: FROM `project.dataset.table`;
17: ```
18: 
19: If the values fall outside the expected years (for example 2019–2020), reload the table from a clean source using a replacement load, preferably Parquet:
20: 
21: ```bash
22: bq load \
23:   --source_format=PARQUET \
24:   --replace \
25:   dataset.table \
26:   gs://bucket/path/*.parquet
27: ```
28: 
29: Note: Using Parquet instead of CSV often helps prevent schema interpretation issues and ensures a cleaner, replace-based reload.

FAQ section: Module 1: Docker
FAQ question: Docker: docker pull dbpage

Document (the answer, with line numbers):
1: Whenever a `docker pull` is performed (either manually or by `docker-compose up`), it attempts to fetch the given image name from a repository. If the repository is public, the fetch and download occur without any issues.
2: 
3: For instance:
4: 
5: ```bash
6: docker pull postgres:13
7: docker pull dpage/pgadmin4
8: ```
9: 
10: **Be Advised:** The Docker images we'll be using throughout the Data Engineering Zoomcamp are all public, unless otherwise specified. This means you are not required to perform a `docker login` to fetch them.
11: 
12: If you encounter the message:
13: 
14: ```
15: docker login': denied: requested access to the resource is denied.
16: ```
17: 
18: This is likely due to a typo in your image name. For instance:
19: 
20: ```bash
21: $ docker pull dbpage/pgadmin4
22: ```
23: 
24: This command will throw an exception:
25: 
26: ```
27: Error response from daemon: pull access denied for dbpage/pgadmin4, repository does not exist or may require 'docker login': denied: requested access to the resource is denied
28: ```
29: 
30: This occurs because the actual image name is `dpage/pgadmin4`, not `dbpage/pgadmin4`.
31: 
32: **How to fix it:**
33: 
34: ```bash
35: $ docker pull dpage/pgadmin4
36: ```
37: 
38: **Extra Notes:** In some professional environments, the Docker image may be in a private repository that your DockerHub username has access to. In this case, you must:
39: 
40: 1. Execute:
41:    ```bash
42:    $ docker login
43:    ```
44: 2. Enter your username and password.
45: 3. Then perform the `docker pull` against that private repository.

FAQ section: Module 7: Streaming
FAQ question: Why does the PyFlink streaming job fail with a JSON deserialization error when consuming records from the Kafka/Redpanda topic?

Document (the answer, with line numbers):
1: Problem
2: The PyFlink streaming job fails during deserialization with a JSON error when consuming records from Kafka/Redpanda. This happens if the produced JSON payload contains NaN values (e.g., NaN in numeric fields like passenger_count). Standard JSON does not allow NaN, so Flink's JSON parser rejects the payload and the source fails, causing the job to restart.
3: 
4: Root cause
5: NaN is not valid JSON. When NaN is serialized into JSON, downstream JSON parsers (including Flink's) fail to parse the record.
6: 
7: Fix
8: Clean the dataset before producing events by replacing NaN values with null or a valid number before serialization.
9: 
10: How to implement (example in Python)
11: ```python
12: import json
13: import math
14: 
15: def sanitize_and_serialize(record):
16:     # Convert NaNs to JSON nulls
17:     for key, value in record.items():
18:         if isinstance(value, float) and math.isnan(value):
19:             record[key] = None
20:     return json.dumps(record, separators=(',', ':'), ensure_ascii=False)
21: 
22: # Example usage
23: # Suppose 'rows' is an iterable of dicts representing taxi trips
24: for row in rows:
25:     json_str = sanitize_and_serialize(row)
26:     # send json_str to Kafka/Redpanda
27: ```
28: 
29: Alternative: simple NaN handling with a default numeric value
30: ```python
31: # If you prefer numeric defaults instead of nulls
32: df = df.fillna({'passenger_count': 0, 'trip_distance': 0, 'fare_amount': 0})
33: ```
34: 
35: Validation
36: - After serialization, verify that the payload is valid JSON:
37: ```python
38: import json
39: json.loads(json_str)  # should not raise
40: ```
41: 
42: Notes
43: - This is the recommended approach; avoid sending NaN in JSON payloads.
44: - If you cannot modify the producer, you may consider additional validation at the ingestion layer, but the source-level sanitization is most reliable.

4:

6:    spark = (SparkSession

10:        .getOrCreate())
11:    
12:    spark.streams.resetTerminated()

16:

18:    query1 = spark

29:

32:        ...

38:

FAQ section: Module 1: Docker
FAQ question: docker on Windows: volume mount path syntax (Git Bash, MINGW, paths with spaces, "ny_taxi_postgres_data is empty")

Document (the answer, with line numbers):
1: Mounting host paths on Windows is the single biggest source of week 1 confusion. Symptoms:
2: 
3: - `ny_taxi_postgres_data` appears empty even though Postgres started.
4: - `Docker: invalid reference format: repository name must be lowercase`
5: - `Error response from daemon: invalid mode: \Program Files\Git\var\lib\postgresql\data`
6: - A folder with a weird name like `ny_taxi_postgres_data;C` is created.
7: 
8: **Root cause**
9: 
10: Git Bash / MINGW64 mangles Unix-style paths into Windows-style paths before passing them to Docker, and the rules differ depending on quoting, leading slashes, and whether your path contains spaces. The cleanest workaround on Windows is to skip the host-bind mount entirely (see [the named-volume FAQ](#0beb2b5df7)) — but if you need the bind mount, here's what tends to work.
11: 
12: **Use a path without spaces**
13: 
14: Move your project out of any directory with spaces (e.g. from `C:\Users\Alexey Grigorev\git\...` to `C:\git\...`). Many of the path-syntax issues simply go away once the path is clean.
15: 
16: **Try these `-v` syntax variants in order**
17: 
18: ```bash
19: # 1. Forward slashes, with leading slash on the drive letter:
20: -v "/c/Users/me/project/ny_taxi_postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data"
21: 
22: # 2. Double leading slashes (some MINGW versions need this):
23: -v "//c/Users/me/project/ny_taxi_postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data"
24: 
25: # 3. With a colon after the drive letter:
26: -v "/c:/Users/me/project/ny_taxi_postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data"
27: 
28: # 4. Backslashes in quotes:
29: -v "c:\Users\me\project\ny_taxi_postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data"
30: 
31: # 5. Use $(pwd) — wrap in quotes:
32: -v "$(pwd)/ny_taxi_postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data"
33: ```
34: 
35: **Also try `winpty`**
36: 
37: If the command appears to do nothing or hangs:
38: 
39: ```bash
40: winpty docker run -it ...
41: ```
42: 
43: **If `Docker: invalid reference format: repository name must be lowercase`**
44: 
45: This usually means the shell didn't substitute `$(pwd)` properly and inserted a literal `\Program Files\Git\...` into the path. Use one of the explicit paths above instead of `$(pwd)`.
46: 
47: **If you see a folder called `ny_taxi_postgres_data;C` get created**
48: 
49: The volume mount string was misparsed. Delete the bogus folder and retry with `//c/...` (double leading slash) instead of `/c/...`.
50: 
51: **On Mac, just wrap `$(pwd)` in quotes**
52: 
53: ```bash
54: docker run -it \
55:   -e POSTGRES_USER=root -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=root -e POSTGRES_DB=ny_taxi \
56:   -v "$(pwd)/ny_taxi_postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data" \
57:   -p 5432:5432 \
58:   postgres:16
59: ```
60: 
61: **Last resort: use a named volume**
62: 
63: If none of the bind-mount syntaxes work, switch to a named volume. The data still persists, you just don't see it in your project folder:
64: 
65: ```bash
66: -v ny_taxi_postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
67: ```
68: 
69: This is the recommended approach on Windows.
